opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that at the scale we're training these models now, you really can't separate the decisions. When you're pre-training a large language model, every choice you make at one layer of the stack ripples into the others. The model architecture affects how well you can shard it across thousands of accelerators. The way you partition the model and the data affects your memory footprint and your communication overhead. That in turn determines what batch size you can use, which feeds back into your optimization choices and your training stability.

When I was working on PaLM, for example, a lot of what made it possible to train a 540-billion-parameter model efficiently came from thinking about the system and the model together. We were training across two TPU pods, and we had to think carefully about how to use data parallelism across the pods and model parallelism within them, and about getting high hardware utilization. If you design the model in isolation and then hand it to someone to "make it run fast," you leave a lot on the table. Sometimes a small architectural tweak, like how you structure the attention and feed-forward layers, or using parallel layers, gives you a meaningful speedup with no loss in quality.

There's also the stability side. When you run a training job for weeks or months on that much hardware, you'll see loss spikes, hardware failures, and numerical issues. Understanding where those come from means understanding the data pipeline, the numerics on the hardware, the optimizer, and the model all at once. If you only understand one piece, you end up debugging blind.

And it goes up the stack too. The data mixture you choose and how you tokenize it shape what capabilities you get downstream, and evaluation tells you whether those choices paid off. So for me, pre-training is fundamentally a co-design problem. The people who are most effective are the ones who can move fluidly between thinking about chips and compilers, distributed systems, model architecture, and data, because the best solutions usually sit at the boundaries between them.

r001.rationale: The response says that training jobs lasting weeks or months require understanding the data pipeline, hardware numerics, optimizer, and model together.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when people think about pre-training, they often think about it as a modeling problem — you pick an architecture, you pick a dataset, you set the hyperparameters, and then you train. But in practice, when you're training at the scale of something like PaLM, with hundreds of billions of parameters across thousands of accelerators, the modeling decisions and the systems decisions are completely intertwined. You can't really separate them.

So, for example, the choice of how you shard the model — whether you're doing data parallelism, model parallelism, pipeline parallelism, or some combination — that's not just an engineering detail. It determines what batch sizes are feasible, what sequence lengths you can afford, how often you're communicating across chips, and ultimately how many useful FLOPs you actually get out of the hardware. If your model FLOPs utilization is low, you're effectively training a smaller model for the same budget. And that feeds right back into the scaling decisions: how big should the model be versus how many tokens should you train on?

And it goes the other direction too. Architectural choices that look innocuous on paper — something like multi-query attention, or using parallel layers where the attention and feedforward blocks compute at the same time — those were partly motivated by what runs efficiently on TPUs at scale. Multi-query attention barely changes training cost, but it makes inference dramatically cheaper, and if you're thinking about actually serving the model, that matters enormously.

Then there's the data pipeline, which people underestimate. At that scale you need deterministic, resumable data loading, because you will have hardware failures, and you need to be able to restart from a checkpoint and know exactly which examples the model has and hasn't seen. Otherwise you can't reproduce anything, and you can't debug things like loss spikes, which we did encounter.

And honestly, the compiler and the runtime matter too. With something like Pathways orchestrating across multiple pods, we had to think about how the computation gets expressed so that the compiler can actually overlap communication and computation. If you only think at the level of the model, you'll make decisions that leave a lot of performance on the table, or worse, you'll hit failures you don't understand.

So I'd say the reason it's essential is that every layer leaks into every other layer. The hardware constrains the systems design, the systems design constrains what models are practical, and the model you want to build pushes back on all of it. The teams that do this well are the ones where the researchers and the systems people are actually in the same conversation, making those trade-offs together rather than handing things over a wall.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains that large-scale pre-training requires thinking across the system, but does not say that the runs last months.

astra-6.text:
Because the choices you make at one layer affect what’s possible at every other layer. When you’re pre-training a large model, you can’t think about the model architecture independently of the hardware, the systems software, or the data pipeline. They all determine how efficiently you can train and how quickly you can learn from experiments.

For example, an architecture might look very promising in terms of model quality, but if it requires a lot of communication across devices, that can become the bottleneck. You have to think about how you partition the model, where the data lives, and how you keep the accelerators busy. Those systems decisions then feed back into which modeling choices are practical.

So, for me, thinking across the stack means looking at the whole training process as a connected problem. The goal is to use the compute you have effectively to build a better model, and that requires the modeling and systems work to inform each other.

r001.rationale: The response explains that pre-training requires considering the model, hardware, software, and data pipeline together, but it does not mention runs lasting months.

sol-6.1.text:
When you’re pre-training a model, the architecture, the training data, the optimization, and the hardware are all connected. A choice that looks good from a modeling perspective might be very inefficient on the system you’re using. And that matters because, with a fixed compute budget, efficiency determines how many experiments you can run and how much data you can train on.

So I think it’s essential to look across those layers together. How do we distribute the computation? Where are we spending time communicating rather than computing? Can we make a different architectural choice that preserves model quality but makes training more efficient? Those are jointly modeling and systems questions. Thinking across the stack lets you make those tradeoffs deliberately and ultimately build a better model with the resources you have.

r001.rationale: The candidate says architecture, data, optimization, and hardware must be considered together and discusses compute-budget efficiency, but it does not state that pre-training runs last months.
